artiest/lindsay-cooper.text:
Lindsay Cooper was an English bassoonist, oboist and composer, born in Hornsey, north London, in 1951. She began piano lessons at the age of eleven and switched to bassoon a few years later. From 1965 to 1968 she studied at Dartington College of Arts and the Royal College of Music and played in the National Youth Orchestra. When she returned to England in 1971 she left classical music and ended up in the Canterbury scene. She joined the progressive rock band Comus. There she added oboe and flute to her instruments and began doing session work for other musicians.

In late 1973 Henry Cow asked her to replace Geoff Leigh, because her classical background offered the group new directions. She played on the second album, Unrest, straight away. From 1977 she was one of the group's most important composers and wrote half of the final album, Western Culture, from 1978. Later she was a member of National Health, News from Babel and David Thomas and the Pedestrians, and she co-founded the Feminist Improvising Group. Records under her own name include Rags in 1980 and Music For Other Occasions in 1986. She also worked with Chris Cutler and the film-maker Sally Potter.

In the late 1970s Cooper was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. She made this public only in the late 1990s, when the illness made live performance impossible for her. She died in 2013. Cooper brought bassoon and oboe into experimental rock, a place where that rarely happened.
artiest/lindsay-cooper.listen: Listen to a track from Rags and notice the bassoon and the oboe among the other instruments. Try to hear how those woodwinds make the sound darker and tighter.

artiest/lindsey-buckingham.text:
Lindsey Buckingham is an American guitarist, singer, songwriter and producer. He was born in Palo Alto, California, in 1949. His first guitar was a Mickey Mouse toy guitar, with which he played along to his older brother's singles. He never had lessons, and he cannot read music. As a teenager he played folk on guitar and banjo. In the school band Fritz he played bass and sang, and he asked his girlfriend Stevie Nicks to join as a singer. As a duo they made the album Buckingham Nicks in 1973, which sold poorly.

When Mick Fleetwood was looking for a new guitarist for Fleetwood Mac in late 1974, he asked Buckingham. He would come only if Nicks could join too, and Fleetwood took them both on. With them the band enjoyed its greatest success. Rumours (1977) became one of the best-selling albums of all time. During the recording Buckingham and Nicks broke up, and Buckingham wrote Go Your Own Way about it. He then steered the band towards the experimental double album Tusk (1979), whose title track features a complete university marching band. In 1987 he left Fleetwood Mac for a solo career, with albums such as Law and Order (1981) and Go Insane (1984). From 1997 to 2018 he played in the band again.

Buckingham plays guitar with his fingers rather than a plectrum, a style that betrays his folk background. As a producer and arranger he gave Fleetwood Mac the polished, layered pop sound that made the band so popular in the 1970s.
artiest/lindsey-buckingham.listen: Listen to Go Your Own Way by Fleetwood Mac and notice Buckingham's fierce, hurried singing, aimed at Stevie Nicks, who sings along in the backing vocals herself. Wait for the end, where he plays a sharp electric guitar solo.

artiest/link-wray.text:
Link Wray, in full Fred Lincoln Wray, was an American guitarist, songwriter and singer. He was born in Dunn, North Carolina, in 1929 and grew up in great poverty. According to him his mother was of Shawnee descent, and the family faced discrimination. With his brothers he played country in clubs around Portsmouth, Virginia. During the Korean War he contracted tuberculosis and a lung had to be removed. Doctors thought he would never be able to sing again, and he turned to instrumental guitar music.

In 1958 Rumble was released, an instrumental that reached the top 20 in America. It was one of the first rock songs with distortion and tremolo on the guitar. To get that raw sound, Wray poked holes in the speaker of his amplifier. Rumble was slang for a fight between youth gangs, and in New York and Boston the song was banned from the radio for fear that it would incite young people. Further hits followed, such as Rawhide and Jack the Ripper. Later he recorded in a converted chicken coop, making records such as Link Wray (1971), and in the late 1970s he toured with the rockabilly singer Robert Gordon. He died in Copenhagen in 2005.

Wray is regarded as the inventor of the power chord: a bare chord of root and fifth, played hard and distorted. His instrumentals were a blueprint for hard rock, punk and heavy metal. Pete Townshend said that without Rumble he would never have picked up a guitar, and Jimmy Page, Iggy Pop and Neil Young also named him as an influence.
artiest/link-wray.listen: Listen to Rumble and notice the heavy, distorted chords that Wray lets ring out slowly, with a trembling tremolo effect. Hear how few notes he needs to create a menacing atmosphere.

artiest/linkin-park.text:
Linkin Park formed in 1996 in Agoura Hills, a suburb of Los Angeles. The band was first called Xero and then Hybrid Theory. In March 1999 the singer Chester Bennington joined. He formed a duo with Mike Shinoda, who rapped and co-produced the music. With the guitarist Brad Delson, the bassist Dave Farrell, the drummer Rob Bourdon and the DJ Joe Hahn, Linkin Park became one of the most successful bands of nu metal.

The debut Hybrid Theory was released in October 2000. In its first year it sold 4.8 million copies, and it became the best-selling album of 2001. In the End reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100. The sound combined heavy guitars with hip-hop and electronics: Hahn scratched and added samples, Shinoda rapped and Bennington sang and screamed. Meteora (2003) sold more than 800,000 copies in its first week. Numb, the closing track, spent twelve weeks at number 1 on the American modern rock chart.

In 2004 Linkin Park made the remix record Collision Course with the rapper Jay-Z. Numb/Encore won a Grammy for best collaboration between rap and vocals. Chester Bennington died on 20 July 2017. In September 2024 the band returned, with the singer Emily Armstrong and the drummer Colin Brittain, and released the album From Zero. Linkin Park showed how far rock and hip-hop had blended into one another around 2000.
artiest/linkin-park.listen: Numb opens with a melody on keys before the heavy guitars come in. In the chorus, listen to how Chester Bennington sings harder and rawer all the time, while that electronic layer keeps running underneath.

artiest/lionel-bart.text:
Lionel Bart was an English writer and composer of pop music and musicals, born Lionel Begleiter in Stepney, London, in 1930, the youngest of seven children of Jewish parents from Galicia. His father was a tailor. As a young man he was a capable painter. His songwriting career began in amateur theatre and at the Unity Theatre. He gained wider fame with pop songs for the young singers of the manager Larry Parnes, such as Living Doll for Cliff Richard and Rock with the Caveman for Tommy Steele. He also advised Parnes to sign Tommy Hicks, who became famous as Tommy Steele.

His greatest work is the musical Oliver! from 1960, for which he wrote the book, music and lyrics himself. Together with his work for Joan Littlewood at the Theatre Royal in Stratford East, he played a major part in the emergence of the British musical in the 1960s. In 1963 he won a Tony Award for best original score, and the 1968 film adaptation won six Oscars, including best picture. He also wrote the title song of the Bond film From Russia with Love and songs such as Far Away for Shirley Bassey and Do You Mind? for Anthony Newley and Andy Williams.

Andrew Lloyd Webber called him the father of the modern British musical. Bart showed that pop songs and the stage could go together, with melodies that stick in the mind.
artiest/lionel-bart.listen: Listen to a recording of the musical Oliver! and notice how the songs tell the story and at the same time work as stand-alone pop songs. Try to spot a chorus that you can sing along to straight away.

artiest/lionel-hampton.text: Lionel Hampton began as a drummer and became the first great jazz soloist on the vibraphone, a metal percussion instrument with shimmering tones. In 1930 he already played vibraphone on a Louis Armstrong record in Los Angeles. Benny Goodman heard him in 1936 and took him into his quartet. From 1940 Hampton led a big band of his own, which had a hit with Flying Home (1942). Illinois Jacquet's tenor sax solo on that record became a model for rhythm and blues. Hampton's band was loud and rousing and lasted for decades; many young musicians, including Dinah Washington and Quincy Jones, got their start in it.
artiest/lionel-hampton.listen: Listen to the vibraphone: short strokes that glow on after the attack.

artiest/lionel-hampton-and-his-orchestra.text:
Lionel Hampton was an American jazz vibraphonist, drummer and bandleader, born in Louisville in 1908 and raised in Chicago. As a teenager he played drums, and in California he worked in the orchestra of Les Hite. When Louis Armstrong hired the band in 1930, he was so impressed by Hampton's vibraphone that he had him play along. In this way Hampton made the instrument popular in jazz. In 1936 Benny Goodman invited him to join his trio, which became a quartet with Teddy Wilson and Gene Krupa. It was one of the first mixed jazz groups to play for audiences.

In 1940 Hampton left Goodman and founded a big band of his own. With that orchestra he recorded Flying Home for Decca on 26 May 1942, in an arrangement by the pianist Milt Buckner. The solo by the saxophonist Illinois Jacquet already pointed to rhythm and blues. The song became Hampton's signature tune. His orchestra became a springboard for young musicians, including Charles Mingus, Wes Montgomery, Dinah Washington, Dizzy Gillespie and Quincy Jones.

The big band played swing with a great deal of energy. At an open-air concert in 1950 the audience nearly went wild when his band marched across the field. His orchestra thus bridged swing and rhythm and blues. In 1996 he received the National Medal of Arts. He died in 2002.
artiest/lionel-hampton-and-his-orchestra.listen: Listen to Flying Home and notice Illinois Jacquet's solo. Can you hear how the rest of the orchestra urges him on?

artiest/lionel-meunier.text:
Lionel Meunier leads Vox Luminis, a Belgian vocal ensemble for early music. Under his direction the group has recorded mainly music of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, often on the Ricercar label and later also on Alpha. Its recording of Heinrich Schütz's Musicalische Exequien became well known, winning a Gramophone Award and a prize at the International Classical Music Awards in 2012. That work is funeral music for voices, one of the finest pieces in the German early Baroque repertoire.

The repertoire is broad. Recordings have appeared of Samuel Scheidt, Domenico Scarlatti and Orlando di Lasso, of motets by Johann Sebastian Bach, Johann Christoph Bach and Johann Michael Bach, and of Requiems by Johann Fux and Johann Kerll. The ensemble also recorded Bach's Actus Tragicus and the album Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott, about Luther and the music of the Reformation. It also performed English Royal Funeral Music in 2013, with works by Morley, Purcell, Tomkins and Weelkes, and in 2018 Henry Purcell's King Arthur.

Vox Luminis shows that a small choir of soloists, without a conductor who puts himself in the foreground, can produce a clear and transparent sound. In this way these recordings have become a reference for the performance of early vocal music.
artiest/lionel-meunier.listen: Listen to Schütz's Musicalische Exequien and notice how the voices alternate and blend. Can you hear how a small group fills a large space?

artiest/lionel-newman.text:
Lionel Newman was an American conductor, pianist and composer of film and television music, born in New Haven, Connecticut, in 1916. He was the youngest of seven brothers from a Russian-Jewish immigrant family. At sixteen he went to Hollywood to conduct for the impresario Earl Carroll. In the 1930s he conducted tours and accompanied Mae West on piano. At eighteen he played with Newman's Society Orchestra on the passenger ship S.S. Rotterdam.

Newman joined 20th Century Fox as a rehearsal pianist, under his brother Alfred Newman. In 1959 he was the studio's music director for television, later also vice president for the music of television and feature films. He worked there for forty-six years and has more than two hundred films to his name, including How to Marry a Millionaire, North to Alaska, Road House and Love Me Tender, Elvis Presley's first film. He was the music director of all of Marilyn Monroe's Fox films, at her request. In 1969 he won an Oscar with Lennie Hayton for best score of a musical film, for Hello Dolly!. Albums such as Kiss Them for Me, Let's Make Love and The Pleasure Seekers let you hear his work.

The Newmans form a dynasty in film music: Lionel was the uncle of Randy, David and Thomas Newman. In 2013 the music department of Fox was named after him, as The Lionel Newman Music Building. He shows how a studio conductor shaped the sound of Hollywood.
artiest/lionel-newman.listen: Listen to music from Let's Make Love and notice the lush strings and brass of a Hollywood orchestra of the 1960s. Can you hear how the music carries the mood of the scene?

artiest/lionel-richie.text:
Lionel Richie was born in 1949 in Tuskegee, Alabama, and grew up on the campus of the Tuskegee Institute. His grandmother was a pianist. He received a tennis scholarship to the institute and played in the marching band. He abandoned studies for the priesthood and chose music, although he could not read or write music. In the 1970s he became known as a songwriter and co-singer of the Motown group the Commodores, with hits such as Easy, Sail On, Three Times a Lady and Still.

In 1981 he wrote and produced Endless Love, a duet with Diana Ross that is among the best-selling singles of all time. His solo career began in 1982 with the album Lionel Richie. The second album, Can't Slow Down from 1983, reached number one on the Billboard 200 and contained the songs All Night Long (All Night) and Hello. In 1985 he co-wrote the charity single We Are the World with Michael Jackson, which won the Grammy for Song of the Year. Can't Slow Down won the Grammy for Album of the Year. Other records include Dancing on the Ceiling in 1985 and Tuskegee in 2012.

Richie became the most important ballad singer of the 1980s, with a warm, soft voice and smooth, melodic arrangements that were both soul and pop. In 2022 he received the Gershwin Prize and a place in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/lionel-richie.listen: Listen to Hello and notice the quiet piano accompaniment and the warm, almost whispered singing. Can you hear how the melody slowly builds towards the chorus?

artiest/lisa-gerrard.text:
Lisa Gerrard is an Australian singer, musician and composer, born in Melbourne in 1961. She grew up in Prahran, a neighbourhood with many Greek residents, and later said that the Mediterranean music coming from the houses strongly influenced her. In Melbourne's experimental post-punk scene, the Little Band scene, she met Brendan Perry. She sang in the post-punk group Microfilm and in 1981 founded Dead Can Dance with Perry, of which she remained a member until 2022. With Perry she explored many traditional and modern styles and laid the foundation for what has come to be called neoclassical dark wave.

Gerrard is known for her remarkable vocal technique, glossolalia, a language of her own without words, with a dramatic contralto and a range of three octaves. She released solo albums such as The Mirror Pool in 1995 and worked on more than forty-eight film scores. For the music of Gladiator from 2000, together with Hans Zimmer, she received a Golden Globe. She also wrote for The Insider, Whale Rider and Balibo, which won an ARIA Award. She also recorded Immortal Memory.

Her voice sounds both ancient and contemporary and has become a fixture in film music, where she conveys emotion without ordinary lyrics.
artiest/lisa-gerrard.listen: Listen to her singing in the music of Gladiator and notice the wordless, flowing voice above the orchestral sound. Can you hear how her voice is used as an instrument?

artiest/lita-ford.text:
Lita Ford is a British-American guitarist and singer, born in London in 1958. Her father was English and her mother Italian. When she was seven the family moved to the United States, eventually to Long Beach, California. Inspired by Ritchie Blackmore of Deep Purple, she began playing guitar at eleven. In 1975, at sixteen, she was recruited by the impresario Kim Fowley for The Runaways, an all-female rock band. It was given a record contract, released a first album in 1976 and in the late 1970s became a successful recording and touring group. Ford's lead guitar became a hallmark of it.

After The Runaways she began a solo career in glam metal. Records from it include Out for Blood in 1983, Dancin' on the Edge in 1984, Lita in 1988, Stiletto in 1990 and Dangerous Curves in 1991. The high point came in the late 1980s. Her greatest success is the single Close My Eyes Forever from 1989, a duet with Ozzy Osbourne, which reached number eight on the charts. Later came Black in 1995 and Living Like a Runaway in 2012. In 2016 she wrote her memoirs, Living Like a Runaway.

Ford showed that a woman could play lead guitar in hard rock, in a world dominated by men. Her voice is a mezzo-soprano and sounds rougher than that of many metal singers.
artiest/lita-ford.listen: Listen to Close My Eyes Forever and notice how her voice and Ozzy Osbourne's alternate above the heavy guitars. Can you hear how a rock ballad can be both heavy and melodic?

artiest/little-eva.text:
Little Eva's real name was Eva Narcissus Boyd. She was born in 1943 in Belhaven, North Carolina. As a teenager she worked as a housekeeper and earned extra money as a babysitter for the songwriting couple Carole King and Gerry Goffin. Her story shows how close writing, recording and releasing lay together in the hit factory of the Brill Building.

Goffin and King wrote The Loco-Motion hoping that Dee Dee Sharp would record it. Sharp did not want to. Eva Boyd had sung the demo, and so she got her chance. Don Kirshner released the song in June 1962 on his label Dimension Records, under the name Little Eva. It became a number 1 in America that year. The backing vocals are by Carole King herself. The lyrics describe a dance, but it did not yet exist: Boyd made up the steps only once the song was a hit. Keep Your Hands Off My Baby (1962) and Let's Turkey Trot (1963) followed. With Big Dee Irwin she sang Swinging on a Star in 1963, although her name was not on the label.

Her own career remained short. The song, however, lived on. Grand Funk Railroad reached number 1 in America with it in 1974. Kylie Minogue had a number 1 with it in Australia in 1987, and a year later a hit in England and America in a version by Stock Aitken Waterman, the hit factory of the 1980s. Eva Boyd died in 2003 in Kinston, North Carolina.
artiest/little-eva.listen: In The Loco-Motion, listen to the backing vocals: that is Carole King, the songwriter herself. Notice also the lyrics, which explain, step by step, a dance that did not yet exist when the song was recorded.

artiest/little-nell.text:
Little Nell is the stage name of Nell Campbell, an Australian actress, singer and former club owner, born in Sydney in 1953. Her father, a writer, called her Little Nell in his column in the Sydney Daily Telegraph, after a character in Charles Dickens's The Old Curiosity Shop. When she arrived in England with her family in the early 1970s, she chose that name as her stage name. She sold clothes at Kensington Market, next to Freddie Mercury's stall, and worked as a street musician and in a café. There her tap dancing was noticed, and that was one reason she got the role of Columbia in the first production of The Rocky Horror Show.

In 1975 she also played Columbia in the film The Rocky Horror Picture Show. She then signed to A&M Records. Her first single was Stilettos and Lipstick with Do the Swim on the B-side, in 1975. In 1978 followed a disco version of Fever and the EP The Musical World of Little Nell. In the British television series Rock Follies of '77 she played Sandra LeMon, in 1981 she was Nurse Ansalong in Shock Treatment and in 1984 Beth in The Killing Fields.

In 1986 she opened the nightclub Nell's in New York, which she owned until 2004 and which became a well-known meeting place. Her contribution to pop history lies mainly in the cult classic Rocky Horror, in which Columbia, with her glittering tap dance, became a fixture.
artiest/little-nell.listen: Listen to Time Warp from The Rocky Horror Picture Show and notice how the group of performers and Columbia's singing together form a festive dance. Can you hear how the music parodies 1950s rock 'n' roll?

artiest/little-richard.text:
Little Richard's real name was Richard Wayne Penniman and he was born on 5 December 1932 in Macon, Georgia. He grew up in a religious family and learned to sing in church, preferably in the Pentecostal congregations with their exuberant services and live music. Gospel singers such as Sister Rosetta Tharpe were his first examples. In 1947 she even let the fourteen-year-old open her concert in Macon.

The breakthrough came in 1955 with Tutti Frutti, which also reached the American and British pop charts. Long Tall Sally became a number 1 on the American rhythm-and-blues chart in 1956, and more hits followed quickly, including Lucille and Good Golly Miss Molly. In 1957 he turned his back on rock 'n' roll and chose religion. Only in 1962 did he allow himself to be persuaded to tour Europe, on which The Beatles were his opening act a few times.

His music revolved around rousing piano playing, a hard backbeat and a raw, powerful voice with high whoops. With capes, turbans and wild performances he was also a showman. He was one of the first Black artists who, in an age of segregation, reached a white and a Black audience at the same time. Elvis Presley, Buddy Holly, Bill Haley and many others recorded his songs, and his way of singing carried on in soul and funk. In 1986 he was among the first group of artists in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He died on 9 May 2020.
artiest/little-richard.listen: Listen to the beginning of Tutti Frutti (1955), where Little Richard shouts a string of nonsense syllables before the band comes in. Then notice the hammering rhythm, the saxophone solo and the high cries with which he keeps rising above the music.

artiest/little-walter.text:
Little Walter, whose real name was Marion Walter Jacobs, was born in Louisiana in 1930 and died in Chicago in 1968. As a child he learned to play the harmonica. At twelve he left home and played on the street in New Orleans, Memphis and St. Louis, among other places, where he travelled with older blues musicians such as Sonny Boy Williamson II. In 1946 he arrived in Chicago. There he stood out with his harmonica playing and played in Muddy Waters's band.

In 1952 he recorded under his own name for Checker Records, a subsidiary of Chess. The first song of his first session, Juke, reached number one on Billboard's R&B chart and stayed at the top for eight weeks. It is still the only harmonica instrumental to have managed that. Between 1952 and 1958 he had fourteen top-ten hits on that chart, including My Babe in 1955. His backing band was called The Aces, with the brothers David and Louis Myers on guitar and Fred Below on drums. He also played on recordings by others, such as Bo Diddley.

He had his harmonica amplified so that it could hold its own against the electric guitars. He set the standard vocabulary for blues and blues-rock harmonica. In 2008 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, as the first and only inductee honoured specifically as a harmonica player. His later years were overshadowed by alcoholism.
artiest/little-walter.listen: Listen to Juke and notice the tone of the amplified harmonica. Can you hear how the band gives it room?

artiest/london-contemporary-orchestra.text:
The London Contemporary Orchestra, LCO for short, was founded in 2008 by Hugh Brunt and Robert Ames. It is an ensemble of young musicians that wants to explore new music and bring it to an ever wider audience. The first season took place at LSO St Luke's and included works by Mark-Anthony Turnage, Kaija Saariaho, Thomas Adès, Iannis Xenakis, Olivier Messiaen and Jonny Greenwood of Radiohead, alongside new pieces by young composers. The orchestra plays on stages and at festivals in Britain and beyond, including at the Roundhouse.

From the beginning the LCO sought the border with pop music and electronics. In 2009 it collaborated with the experimental duo Matmos and the composer Anna Meredith. In 2010 it played works by Steve Reich, John Cage and Biosphere, and in 2013 it performed Claude Vivier in the disused Aldwych Underground station, a hundred metres below ground. In 2015 it won the ensemble prize at the Royal Philharmonic Society Music Awards. In January 2022 it played a non-stop twenty-four-hour concert at the Barbican Centre.

The orchestra also contributed to film music. In 2018 it played on Thom Yorke's first film score, for Suspiria, and later it worked with Jed Kurzel on films such as The Mustang and Seberg. Albums such as LAGEOS from 2018 and Spiderhead from 2022 show that bridge. The LCO shows that a string orchestra is also at home in the pop world, alongside Radiohead and electronic musicians.
artiest/london-contemporary-orchestra.listen: Listen to the film music of Suspiria and notice how the strings and the voices together create a menacing atmosphere. Can you hear how an orchestra can sound like an electronic instrument?

artiest/london-grammar.text:
London Grammar is an English indie pop band that formed in Nottingham in 2009. The singer Hannah Reid and the guitarist Dan Rothman, both from London, met in their first year at the University of Nottingham. A year later Dominic Major joined, who plays keyboards, djembe and drums. After their studies they moved to London and played in small cafés. In 2012 they signed to Ministry of Sound, and in the studio they worked with Rollo Armstrong of Faithless and Liam Howe of Sneaker Pimps, among others.

In 2013 the EP Metal & Dust and the single Wasting My Young Years were released. In September of that year the debut album If You Wait came out, with Strong as its biggest hit. Strong won an Ivor Novello Award and entered the Top 2000 in 2014. Their cover of Nightcall also stood out. The following albums, Truth Is a Beautiful Thing (2017), made with producers such as Paul Epworth and Greg Kurstin, and Californian Soil (2021), both reached number one in England. In 2024 The Greatest Love followed.

London Grammar's music is calm and spacious, with elements of ambient and classical music, melancholy guitar and influences of trip-hop and dance. At the centre is Hannah Reid's powerful, clear voice. Reid writes the lyrics and vocal lines, Major devises piano parts and Rothman adds guitar. In this way the band shows how the dark, slow mood of 1990s trip-hop lives on in the pop music of a later generation.
artiest/london-grammar.listen: Listen to Strong and notice how bare the accompaniment is: a few piano chords, a restrained guitar and only later a slow beat. Hear how Hannah Reid's voice gets all the room above it and grows higher and fuller.

artiest/london-philharmonic-orchestra.text:
The London Philharmonic Orchestra, LPO for short, is a British orchestra founded in London in 1932 by the conductors Sir Thomas Beecham and Malcolm Sargent. It was intended as a rival to the existing London Symphony Orchestra and the BBC Symphony Orchestra. The founders wanted to build an orchestra that could match any European or American competitor. Between 1932 and the Second World War, by the judgement of most assessors, they succeeded. When the war began, the private backers withdrew, and the players turned the LPO into a self-governing cooperative.

In the 1960s the orchestra regained its old standard, and in 1964 it received an important appointment at the Glyndebourne summer festival. In 1993 it became the resident orchestra of the Royal Festival Hall on the Thames. Since Beecham, its principal conductors have included Sir Adrian Boult, Bernard Haitink, Sir Georg Solti, Klaus Tennstedt and Vladimir Jurowski, and since 2021 it has been Edward Gardner. The LPO has worked in recording studios since its beginnings and recorded hundreds of works for EMI, Decca and other labels. The list of records includes Peter and the Wolf from 1949, Messiah from 1956 and The Planets from 1956.

The LPO is therefore one of the best-known sounds of London, both in the concert hall and on record. The orchestra brought large parts of the symphonic repertoire to a wide audience, far beyond the British borders as well.
artiest/london-philharmonic-orchestra.listen: Listen to The Planets and notice how the brass and percussion set up a menacing rhythm in the opening movement. Try to hear how the sound changes when the strings take over.

artiest/london-sinfonietta.text:
The London Sinfonietta is an English chamber orchestra for contemporary music, founded in 1968 and based in London. David Atherton and Nicholas Snowman founded it. Atherton was the first music director, and Snowman the first general manager. In the first concert on 24 January 1968 the ensemble gave the world premiere of John Tavener's The Whale. In 1970 it recorded that work for The Beatles' label, Apple Records. Since then the London Sinfonietta has commissioned more than three hundred new works and given many hundreds of premieres.

The core consists of eighteen regular players. Later the ensemble was led by Michael Vyner, Paul Crossley, Markus Stenz and Oliver Knussen, among others. It is resident orchestra at the Southbank Centre and artistic partner of Kings Place. The recordings form a catalogue of twentieth-century classics, such as Berio Conducts Berio from 1977, Harrison Birtwistle's Verses for Ensembles and Clarinet Concertos from 1981.

In the early years classical repertoire was also on the programme; later it focused mainly on music from the last decades of the twentieth century. In the 2000s the ensemble sought collaboration with pop and electronic artists, in order to link the sound worlds of different genres. In this way the London Sinfonietta shows that new classical music and pop music can meet, even though the project began with a composition that The Beatles released.
artiest/london-sinfonietta.listen: Listen to Berio Conducts Berio and notice how the small ensemble of winds, strings and percussion keeps making different colours. Can you hear how every player in this ensemble has a role of his own?

artiest/london-symphony-orchestra.text:
The London Symphony Orchestra, LSO for short, was founded in 1904 and is the oldest symphony orchestra in London. A group of players left Henry Wood's Queen's Hall Orchestra, because a new rule obliged them to work exclusively for that orchestra. The LSO later introduced a similar rule itself. The orchestra is self-governing and chooses the conductors it works with. In the early years these were mainly Hans Richter, Sir Edward Elgar and Sir Thomas Beecham, later Pierre Monteux and André Previn, among others.

In the 1930s and 1950s the LSO was overshadowed by newer orchestras, first by the BBC Symphony Orchestra and the London Philharmonic Orchestra, then by the Philharmonia and the Royal Philharmonic. In the 1960s it recovered its leading position. In 1966 the LSO Chorus was added for choral works. Since 1982 the orchestra has been based at the Barbican Centre, where it has held large festivals devoted to composers such as Berlioz, Mahler and Leonard Bernstein. The LSO calls itself the most recorded orchestra in the world. It has made gramophone records since 1912 and played on more than two hundred film soundtracks. The list includes the Warsaw Concerto from 1942, The Planets from 1954 and Messiah from 1956.

Through that recording and film work the LSO reached an audience that never set foot in a concert hall. Classical music and film thus came together, and the orchestra became one of the most recognisable British sounds.
artiest/london-symphony-orchestra.listen: Listen to the Warsaw Concerto and notice how the piano and the orchestra alternate in a romantic, cinematic theme. Can you hear how the orchestra envelops the piano?

artiest/london-symphony-orchestra-en-cla.text:
Alexander Nevsky is a work by Sergei Prokofiev from 1938, the music for Sergei Eisenstein's film about the Russian prince who defeated the German knights in the thirteenth century. The Battle on the Ice is the best-known part. Prokofiev also made a cantata of the music. This performance is by the London Symphony Orchestra under Claudio Abbado, who was that orchestra's principal conductor from 1979 to 1987.

Claudio Abbado was born in Milan in 1933 and died in 2014. He studied piano, composition and conducting, became principal conductor of La Scala in Milan in 1969 and later led the Wiener Staatsoper and the Berliner Philharmoniker, among others. From 1975 to 1979 he was principal guest conductor of the London Symphony Orchestra and then, from 1979 to 1987, principal conductor, and from 1984 also music director. He also founded youth orchestras, such as the European Union Youth Orchestra and the Gustav Mahler Jugendorchester.

Abbado was known for his Mahler and his attention to contemporary music.
artiest/london-symphony-orchestra-en-cla.listen: Listen to The Battle on the Ice and notice how the orchestra builds tension. When does the tension rise?

artiest/lonnie-donegan.text:
Lonnie Donegan, born Anthony James Donegan in Glasgow in 1931, was the British singer and guitarist who became known as the King of Skiffle. With his hits he inspired thousands of British teenagers in the second half of the 1950s to start a band of their own, among them the future Beatles.

Donegan began in British trad jazz, as a banjo player with Ken Colyer and then in the band of the trombonist Chris Barber. In the intervals of the concerts he played American folk and blues numbers with two band members, with guitar, washboard and bass: the skiffle break. In July 1954 Donegan recorded Rock Island Line in this way, a song about a railway line that he knew from the blues musician Lead Belly. Barber played double bass, Beryl Bryden washboard. Donegan sang it at a fast tempo. At the end of 1955 the song was released as a single on Decca. In early 1956 it became a top 10 hit in England and also entered the American top 10. It was the first British debut record to go gold. Dozens of hits followed, including the number 1 hits Gamblin' Man (1957) and My Old Man's a Dustman (1960).

Skiffle demanded little: a cheap guitar, a washboard and a bass made from a tea chest. That made it the do-it-yourself music of the 1950s. John Lennon started the skiffle band The Quarrymen in Liverpool, and Paul McCartney and George Harrison later named Donegan as an early influence. Through skiffle, British youngsters got to know American blues and folk, the music they sold back to America in the 1960s in the British Invasion.
artiest/lonnie-donegan.listen: In Rock Island Line, listen to how it builds: Donegan begins as a storyteller, with a spoken intro about the railway line, and then launches into the song, fast and driven like a moving train. The washboard provides the rattling rhythm that is so typical of skiffle.

artiest/lonnie-liston-smith.text:
Lonnie Liston Smith is an American jazz pianist and keyboardist, born in Richmond, Virginia, in 1940. His father sang in a gospel group. Smith came to New York in 1963, where he played with Betty Carter, Roland Kirk and Art Blakey, among others, and then with Pharoah Sanders in a band that sought the edge of free jazz. On Sanders's album Thembi he touched a Fender Rhodes for the first time. Later he also worked with Gato Barbieri and Miles Davis.

In 1973 he formed his own group, Lonnie Liston Smith and the Cosmic Echoes. The albums Cosmic Funk from 1974, Expansions from 1974 and Visions of a New World from 1975 contain a calm fusion of jazz, soul and funk, with dreamy vocals, long spacey instrumental passages, a solid bass line and light percussion. The lyrics and titles carry a message of peace. Smith said that he wanted to expand the consciousness of humankind.

This style attracted an audience outside jazz. His music later became a staple of jazz-funk, chill jazz and acid jazz. In the 1990s hip-hop artists discovered him, among them Guru. Expansions can be heard in the computer games Grand Theft Auto: Vice City and Driver: Parallel Lines. In 2023 he released his first new recording in twenty-five years.
artiest/lonnie-liston-smith.listen: Listen to Expansions and notice the electric piano above the light percussion and the round bass line. Which instruments carry the rhythm?

artiest/lord-flea.text:
Lord Flea was the stage name of Norman Byfield Thomas, a Jamaican mento musician from Kingston, who died in 1959. He began in the dance halls of Kingston and in 1949 was given a regular spot for a year after winning talent contests. With the support of local businessmen he made records. The owner of Club Calypso in Miami was looking in Jamaica for an authentic sound and offered him and his band, the Calypsonians, a residency of several months in the United States.

The music was sold as calypso, but Flea called his style mento. In 1957 he explained that this name was used in Jamaica until calypso became a catch-all name for all West Indian music. The band members had colourful names such as Count Slick, Count Spoon and Prince Charles, and the bassist Fish Ray already used a walking bass. In 1957 the group appeared on The Perry Como Show, recorded the album Swingin' Calypsos for Capitol and played in the films Calypso Joe and Bop Girl Goes Calypso. With Shake Shake Sonora he received a good review in Billboard.

His lyrics are funny. In Mister Give Me Ma Rent, for example, he sings about a nosy landlady. Flea fell ill and died in 1959. His funeral procession was at the time the longest that Miami-Dade had ever seen. He helped set off the calypso craze in the United States, although American imitators made more money from it.
artiest/lord-flea.listen: Listen to Naughty Little Flea and notice how the lyrics tell a funny story over a light, swaying rhythm. What accompaniment do you hear under the singing?

artiest/lord-kitchener.text:
Aldwyn Roberts, better known as Lord Kitchener or Kitch, was born in Arima, Trinidad, in 1922 and died in 2000. His father taught him to sing and play guitar. In 1943 he moved to Port of Spain, where the calypsonian Growling Tiger gave him the name Lord Kitchener. He was known as an innovator who changed both music and lyrics.

In 1948 he travelled to England with Lord Beginner and Lord Woodbine. On his arrival at Tilbury he sang the specially written London Is the Place for Me, live in a Pathé News report. Within two years he was a regular guest at the BBC. For the first five thousand West Indian migrants he became an important figure, because his songs were about the home they longed for. He also wrote Victory Calypso about the West Indies cricket team's first victory over England. In 1962 he returned to Trinidad, where he dominated the calypso competitions with the Mighty Sparrow. Between 1963 and 1976 he won the Road March ten times, more often than anyone else.

In 1977 he recorded Sugar Bum Bum, one of the first big soca hits. For thirty years he ran his own calypso tent, where Calypso Rose and David Rudder developed. There is a statue of him in Port of Spain. He was regarded as the grand master of calypso.
artiest/lord-kitchener.listen: Listen to London Is the Place for Me and notice what the lyrics say about arriving in London. Which instruments accompany him?

artiest/lorenz-hart.text:
Lorenz Hart was an American lyricist and one half of the Broadway team Rodgers and Hart. He was born in Harlem, New York, in 1895, the elder of two sons of German-Jewish immigrants. Through his mother he was a great-nephew of the poet Heinrich Heine. His parents took him to Yiddish and German plays. He was well read from an early age, published poems in student magazines and wrote comic revues at summer camp. He studied at Columbia College and for two years attended the Columbia University School of Journalism.

In 1918 he translated German stage songs into English for the Shubert brothers. In 1919 he met Richard Rodgers, and together they first wrote for amateur and student productions. Their song Any Old Place With You appeared in the musical A Lonely Romeo. In a little over twenty years they wrote music and lyrics for twenty-six Broadway musicals. Their four best known are Babes in Arms, The Boys from Syracuse, Pal Joey and On Your Toes. They also wrote for films, such as Love Me Tonight from 1932. Hart wrote Blue Moon, The Lady Is a Tramp, Manhattan, Bewitched, Bothered and Bewildered and My Funny Valentine, among others.

His lyrics were intimate and proved suited to a long life outside the theatre. Many of them have become standards that singers and jazz musicians keep playing. When Rodgers began a new musical with Oscar Hammerstein in 1942, Hart was already almost out of the picture. He died in 1943.
artiest/lorenz-hart.listen: Listen to My Funny Valentine and notice the lyrics: a love song that sounds not sweet but almost teasing. Can you hear how the words carry the melody?

artiest/lorne-balfe.text: Lorne Balfe was born in Inverness, Scotland, in 1976. With a music scholarship he went to Fettes College in Edinburgh. He worked for a long time at Remote Control Productions, Hans Zimmer's studio, and gained experience there with large film and game projects. For games he wrote the music for Assassin's Creed: Revelations and Assassin's Creed III, among others. For his game music he received several BAFTA nominations. In film he wrote The Lego Batman Movie (2017) and, for the director Christopher McQuarrie, Mission: Impossible – Fallout (2018) and Dead Reckoning Part One (2023). For television he made His Dark Materials (2019–2022), among others. He also wrote the music for Wallace & Gromit: Vengeance Most Fowl (2024).
artiest/lorne-balfe.listen: Notice the short, repeated string ostinatos and heavy percussion accents beneath a simple theme in brass or choir, typical of the Remote Control sound.

artiest/los-angeles-azules.text:
Los Ángeles Azules is a Mexican group that plays cumbia, the Mexican variant of that musical style. The name means the blue angels. The group came together in 1976 and began officially in 1980. It was formed by the siblings of the Mejía Avante family: Elías, Alfredo, José Hilario, Jorge, Cristina and Guadalupe.

The group went through several periods of popularity. A big hit came in 1997 with Cómo te voy a olvidar. In 2013 it re-recorded many of its successes with guest singers such as Carla Morrison, Lila Downs and Ximena Sariñana. In 2014 it began with cumbia sinfónica, in which the hits were played with the Mexico City Symphony Orchestra. The album De plaza en plaza from 2016 contains collaborations with Gloria Trevi, Yuri, Natalia Lafourcade, Miguel Bosé and Ha*Ash. In 2018 Esto sí es cumbia appeared, made up entirely of covers.

In 2018 the group played at the Coachella festival, the first time a traditional cumbia group performed there. The music is made for dancing. In this way the family brought a popular dance style to festivals and concert halls.
artiest/los-angeles-azules.listen: Listen to Cómo te voy a olvidar and notice the danceable cumbia rhythm and the melody of the singing. Which instruments do you hear most clearly?

artiest/los-incas.text:
Los Incas is an Andean music group that formed in Paris in 1956. Argentine and Venezuelan musicians founded it. Since the early 1960s the group has been led by the Argentine Jorge Milchberg, who plays the charango and was originally a classically trained pianist. It is also known as Urubamba.

In 1965 Simon & Garfunkel and Los Incas both performed at the Théâtre de l'Est parisien, after which a friendship arose between Paul Simon and the group. There the group also played an instrumental version of El Cóndor Pasa. The piece goes back to the Peruvian composer Daniel Alomía Robles, who wrote the music in 1913. Simon added If I Could to the title and wrote lyrics for it. Los Incas accompanied the duo on Bridge Over Troubled Water. The song became a worldwide hit, and the group's own version reached number five in the Top 40 in 1970.

Later the group played on Paul Simon's Duncan and in the early 1970s toured with him under the name Urubamba. Until 1982 albums appeared under that name, after which it went back to Los Incas. The line-up includes the quena, the charango and the guitar. In this way the group brought Andean music to a Western audience.
artiest/los-incas.listen: Listen to El Cóndor Pasa and notice the flute and the plucked charango. Which instruments carry the melody?

artiest/los-kjarkas.text:
Los Kjarkas is a Bolivian group from Capinota in Cochabamba and one of the most popular Andean folk groups in the country's history. The name comes from Quechua and means brave. The leader has always been the singer, guitarist and songwriter Gonzalo Hermosa González. He founded the group with his brothers Élmer and Ulises, Gastón Guardia Bilboa and Ramiro de la Zerda. The group plays styles such as saya, caporal, tuntuna, huayno and carnavales, with instruments such as charango, quena, zampoña, ronroco, guitar and bombo.

In the mid-1980s the group was at its peak. A plagiarism case followed. In 1989 the French group Kaoma made the dance Lambada popular, but that song turned out to be an unauthorised adaptation of Llorando se fue, written by Ulises and Gonzalo Hermosa and sung by Los Kjarkas as a saya. A French court recognised the rights of Los Kjarkas, and Kaoma had to pay substantial damages. The case made the group better known in Europe, Asia and America. The song has since been sampled by others, including in On the Floor by Jennifer Lopez.

Ulises Hermosa died in 1992. The group founded two schools for Andean music, in Lima and Ecuador, and wrote more than three hundred songs. In this way it passed the folk music of the Andes on to a new generation and took it to a worldwide audience.
artiest/los-kjarkas.listen: Listen to Llorando se fue and notice the rhythm of the saya. Which Andean instruments do you hear?

artiest/los-mirlos.text:
Los Mirlos, Spanish for the blackbirds, is a Peruvian cumbia band from Moyobamba in the Peruvian Amazon region. The group formed when several founders moved from Moyobamba to Lima in 1972. A year later it signed to the label Infopesa, for which it released nine albums and two compilations.

The music of Los Mirlos is influenced by psychedelic rock and surf rock, alongside cumbia. The members name groups such as Los Destellos and Los Chamas as important examples. Some simply see the music as psychedelic cumbia. The group emphasised its origins in the Amazon region, including in the titles of albums such as El Milagro Verde from 1975. The founders included the singer Jorge Rodríguez Grández, the guitarists Danny Fardy Johnston and Gilberto Reátegui, and the bassist Manuel Linares.

In 2022 a documentary about the band, Mirlo's Dance, premiered at the Lima film festival. It reached Peruvian cinemas in 2024 and won a prize at the Trujillo film festival. The work of Los Mirlos shows how cumbia could be blended with rock into a style of its own.
artiest/los-mirlos.listen: Listen to La danza de los mirlos and notice the electric guitar that leads the melody. Which instruments play the rhythm?

artiest/lou-donaldson.text:
Lou Donaldson was an American jazz saxophonist, born in Badin, North Carolina, in 1926 and died in 2024. He was known for his soulful, bluesy alto playing, although in his younger years he was strongly influenced by Charlie Parker. In the Second World War he served in the navy in Chicago, where he came into contact with bebop. In 1952 he made his first jazz recordings with Milt Jackson and Thelonious Monk. In 1954 he played in Art Blakey's quintet, with Horace Silver and Clifford Brown, at the recordings at Birdland for the live album A Night at Birdland.

Donaldson recorded many albums for Blue Note, such as Blues Walk and Gravy Train. As a bandleader he gave young musicians such as Grant Green and Lonnie Smith a first chance. In 1967 he returned to Blue Note with a new band, with the guitarist George Benson and the organist Lonnie Smith. The 1967 album Alligator Bogaloo opened with a piece that arose from a spontaneous improvisation and became a signature tune of his. The album fitted soul jazz.

He was regarded as a pioneer of both hard bop and soul jazz. His recordings have often been sampled. In 2012 he was inducted into the North Carolina Music Hall of Fame and named an NEA Jazz Master. In this way he linked bebop with the danceable jazz of the 1960s.
artiest/lou-donaldson.listen: Listen to Alligator Bogaloo and notice the groove of the organ and drums with the bluesy alto saxophone sound above it. Can you hear how the rhythm keeps going while the soloists change?

artiest/lou-reed.text:
Lou Reed was an American musician, songwriter and poet. He was born in Brooklyn in 1942 and grew up in Freeport, on Long Island. He learned to play guitar from the radio and played in garage bands as a teenager. At Syracuse University he studied English with the poet Delmore Schwartz, who taught him that a great deal can be achieved with very simple language. There he also made radio programmes with doo-wop, rhythm and blues and free jazz. In 1964 he went to work in New York writing songs for Pickwick Records.

Through a makeshift band he met John Cale, who played viola in La Monte Young's ensemble. Together with Sterling Morrison and later the drummer Moe Tucker, they formed The Velvet Underground in 1965. Andy Warhol became their manager and brought in the German singer Nico. The debut The Velvet Underground & Nico (1967) sold poorly, but later grew into one of the most influential rock records. Reed sang about drugs, the street and the people around Warhol's Factory, in a flat, almost speaking voice. In 1970 he left. His second solo album Transformer (1972), produced by David Bowie, contained his biggest hit, Walk on the Wild Side. Later came Berlin (1973), New York (1989) and, with Cale, the tribute to Warhol, Songs for Drella (1990).

Reed wanted to bring the sensitivity of a novel to rock music. His lyrics were poetic and abrasive, his guitar playing often experimental and noisy. The Velvet Underground had little success in its own time, but is seen as the foundation of punk, new wave and alternative rock. Reed died in 2013.
artiest/lou-reed.listen: Listen to Walk on the Wild Side and notice the bass line that slides back and forth, and the backing singers with their doo-do-doo. Hear how Reed, almost talking, narrates over it about the people from Warhol's world, and how at the end a saxophone takes over.

artiest/louis-andriessen.text: Louis Andriessen came from a family of composers in Utrecht and for years taught at the Royal Conservatoire in The Hague. He rejected the symphony orchestra as a bourgeois institution and wrote for ensembles of his own with winds, electric guitars and pianos, which play loudly and without vibrato. In De Staat from 1976 four women's voices sing texts by Plato about the dangerous power of music. In this way he laid the foundation for what came to be called the Hague School.
artiest/louis-andriessen.listen: Listen to the beginning of De Staat and hear how oboes and hard chords play in a tight, repeating rhythm, without string vibrato or soft transitions.

artiest/louis-armstrong.text: Louis Armstrong grew up poor in New Orleans and learned to play the cornet in a home for boys. King Oliver became his mentor and brought him to Chicago in 1922. After a period in New York with Fletcher Henderson, Armstrong made the recordings of his Hot Five and Hot Seven between 1925 and 1928. On them the solo became the heart of jazz: long, logical lines with a big tone and a free treatment of the beat. On West End Blues (1928) he opens with a cadenza that musicians still study. With his raw voice and his scat singing he was also a hugely influential singer. Later he became a worldwide star.
artiest/louis-armstrong.listen: Listen to the opening of West End Blues: a trumpet telling a story all alone.

artiest/louis-armstrong-and-his-hot-five.text:
The Hot Five was the first jazz band that Louis Armstrong led under his own name for recordings. In its line-up it was a typical New Orleans band: trumpet, clarinet and trombone, supported by a rhythm section. In that style the three horns together played the leading role, with collective improvisation: the trumpet had the melody and the clarinet and trombone played improvised parts around it. The group was set up at the suggestion of Richard M. Jones for Okeh Records, and all the records were made in Okeh's studio in Chicago.

There were in fact two groups with that name. The first recorded from 1925 to 1927 and consisted of Armstrong's wife, the pianist Lil Hardin Armstrong, and of New Orleans musicians with whom he had played in the 1910s: Kid Ory on trombone, Johnny Dodds on clarinet and Johnny St. Cyr on guitar and banjo. In 1928 Armstrong replaced everyone except himself with members of Carroll Dickerson's orchestra, including Earl Hines on piano and Zutty Singleton on drums. Famous recordings are Cornet Chop Suey, Muskrat Ramble, Hotter Than That and Struttin' with Some Barbecue.

The group's ensemble playing is often strong, but it is above all the playing of Armstrong's cornet or trumpet that defines almost every recording. Those records made the soloist the star of jazz, rather than the group. In doing so they pointed the way to the jazz of later decades.
artiest/louis-armstrong-and-his-hot-five.listen: Listen to Struttin' with Some Barbecue and notice how the trumpet carries the melody while clarinet and trombone play around it. Can you hear the moment when Armstrong takes a solo?

artiest/louis-armstrong-and-his-orchestr.text:
Louis Armstrong and His Orchestra was the name under which the trumpeter and singer Louis Armstrong made records from the 1930s with a big orchestra behind him. Armstrong was born in New Orleans in 1901 and was given the nicknames Satchmo and Pops. In the 1920s he became known as an inventive trumpeter and cornettist. He changed jazz for good: where musicians had previously mostly improvised together, with him the soloist became central.

With his orchestra Armstrong aimed at a large audience. He played not only jazz but also popular songs, such as Irving Berlin's Alexander's Ragtime Band, which he recorded in 1937. His voice was just as important as his trumpet. It sounded raw and hoarse, and he treated words and melody freely, as if he were playing a solo with his voice. He was also a master of scat, singing with sounds without words. The orchestra provided a solid, swinging backdrop, above which Armstrong sang and let his trumpet blare.

Armstrong was one of the first Black entertainers to reach a broad white audience in the divided America of his time. He said little about politics, but during the crisis over school segregation in Little Rock he took a public stand. His career ran from the 1920s to the 1960s, and he kept playing songs such as When the Saints Go Marching In. He died in 1971. His influence reaches far beyond jazz, into the whole of American popular music.
artiest/louis-armstrong-and-his-orchestr.listen: Listen to Alexander's Ragtime Band from 1937. Notice how Armstrong plays with words and melody, and how he and the orchestra make a song from 1911 swing.

artiest/louis-armstrong-s-hot-five.text:
Louis Armstrong's Hot Five was the recording band with which the trumpeter made jazz history under his own name in the 1920s. The group began in 1925 in Chicago, at the suggestion of Richard M. Jones, for the label Okeh Records. It played New Orleans jazz: trumpet, clarinet and trombone in collective improvisation, with a rhythm section underneath. In this way the band captured a style that had arisen in the clubs of New Orleans, and which was now put on record for a large audience.

The first Hot Five consisted of Armstrong, his wife Lil Hardin Armstrong on piano, Kid Ory on trombone, Johnny Dodds on clarinet and Johnny St. Cyr on guitar and banjo. After its success Okeh offered a five-year contract, and in December 1927 followed the session with Struttin' With Some Barbeque, in which Lonnie Johnson also took part on guitar and vocals. In 1928 the band was renewed with Fred Robinson, Jimmy Strong, Earl Hines, Mancy Carr and Zutty Singleton, all from Carroll Dickerson's orchestra. Armstrong was the only musician in both groups.

The Hot Five's records show how Armstrong made the role of the soloist in jazz ever more important. His trumpet playing touches almost every recording, from Cornet Chop Suey to Hotter Than That. In this way they became a source for almost all the jazz musicians who came after them.
artiest/louis-armstrong-s-hot-five.listen: Listen to Hotter Than That and notice how Armstrong both plays trumpet and sings scat. Can you hear how his voice and his instrument resemble each other?
